articles.title: Claire Throssell on 12 years of campaigning for justice for her sons
articles.summary: Jack and Paul were 12 and 9 when their father killed them during a contact visit despite concerns.
articles.body:
Claire Throssell missed seeing her sons by five minutes. She was on her way back from work when they set off for a visit to see their father.

When police knocked on her door later that night, her first thought was: "What has he done?"

Her estranged husband, Darren Sykes, had started a fire in his home while Jack, 12, and Paul, nine, were inside the attic looking at a train set, then locked them in.

The unsupervised access visit had been sanctioned by the family court despite evidence that Sykes had abused both his sons and Claire, and was capable of harming them.

Paul died on that same night, 22 October 2014, and Jack passed away a few days later, believing he had saved his younger brother's life.

Claire made Jack a promise while he lay in her arms in hospital - and this week she feels like, more than a decade on, she kept that promise.

Claire, from Penistone near Barnsley, has spent 12 years campaigning to change the law around presumption of parental involvement, which assumes children benefit from contact with both parents after separation, and on Tuesday she saw the Courts and Tribunals Bill go through its final stages in the Commons.

That means it will become the law she has spent so long fighting for.

I remember sitting in her front room more than a decade ago, nearly a year to the day after the boys were killed.

Some people's nightmares stay with you for a long time.

But Claire has gone through what happened to her, Jack and Paul, thousands of times, in incredibly intricate detail, with hundreds of different journalists.

All because she wanted to keep doing her best to keep her promise.

"There are many days when they are dark. I can sit and think 'how do I get through the next minute?' Never mind the next hour or the next day.

"But then I remind myself that that are dozens of children that don't have that day tomorrow and I've kind of made it my mission to try and educate other people.

"For anyone at risk of harm there is only today, there is no tomorrow and if we can do something better, do it today."

Twelve years on, 2026 marks the year that Jack has been dead for as long as he was alive.

"The right thing to do is love. The right thing to do is take the boys' love and move it forward and share it with the world. Make difference in their names and make a legacy that will last," Claire explains.

"This year, Jack will have been sleeping as long as he was alive. It never feels like a victory, how can it because the boys are not here anymore.

"But it does fell like this is a step to the future, to give generations of children to come, a safe, happy life, free from fear."

Looking back, Claire now realises that Sykes, who also died in the fire, had been manipulative and controlling throughout their relationship.

After they met through work, there were too many flowers, too many phone calls, too much interest in where she was.

That turned into insults, shouting and physical abuse. His behaviour got worse after they married and had Jack and Paul.

By 2014, she had left and moved in with her mother. Custody of the boys was shared.

The boys told social workers that they were scared of their father. Paul told them he was "pure nasty".

Claire also had tried to tell authorities that she was scared of what Sykes was capable of.

She submitted statements to the courts that he'd told her "he had nothing to live for" and that he could "understand fathers killing their children".

His access to his children was limited - but, crucially, unsupervised visits were still allowed.

One of those visits was after school on the day of the fire.

Claire had dropped Jack and Paul off at school that morning, with a call of "I love you" to the pair as they walked away.

Jack, a Toy Story fan, responded with his usual "to infinity and beyond," mimicking the catchphrase of the Buzz Lightyear character from the movie.

She noticed that Jack, who normally looked back at her while he was going into school, turned and looked a second time and issued the same line as his brother.

Their father had texted that morning saying the boys could play with the train set in the attic.

He said he had "two new trains. all he needed was two drivers".

Later he set up the track and then lit 14 separate fires, making sure they could not escape. Jack tried to drag Paul towards the attic door, and was found on the landing.

He was able to tell a firefighter who rescued him: "My dad did this and he did it on purpose."

Jack's determination to make sure people knew the truth while he was still able to tell them has driven Claire on.

"What I've done in the many dark times in the last 12 years is I've taken Jack's courage. The fact he made a conscious decision to think about other people even though he was dying.

"He thought he'd saved his brother's life."

Paul was alive until Claire arrived at Sheffield Children's Hospital.

She says he smiled at her then the light went out of his eyes.

Jack was taken to hospital in Manchester, but died as Claire held him five days later.

It was the same day he had been due to have an interview with family court representatives about his father.

Claire believes that changing the family court presumption, that children should have contact with both parents, will save lives.

"This is not aimed at good parents. This will not affect good parents. This will not affect their access to their children. It will not affect their rights.

"What it will do is look at an abuser that's known to the courts and will say 'you don't have automatic access to your children'.

Not everyone agrees with Claire, The Conservatives tabled an amendment which attempted to keep presumption of contact.

In the debate, South West Devon MP Rebecca Smith MP questioned why the removal of the presumption was needed.

"Courts already have the power to restrict unsafe contact. The presumption of parental contact is already qualified by risk of harm to the child, so why do we need this clause at all?

"In some cases this would increase the state's power to erase one parent from a child's life and we know that is often their father."

Claire says that removing the presumption puts children at the front of decision-making - which would keep them safer.

She also says the Conservative government was told in 2020 that the presumption of contact needed an urgent review.

Ultimately the removal of presumption of contact was voted through.

Claire was in the public gallery of the Commons this week, holding a photograph of her sons and said the feeling was "absolutely incredible".

"I felt Jack and Paul. I couldn't quite believe what I'd heard.

"I've talked about hope and how if you don't have hope you have nothing. If you can't hope that things are going to get better in your life then you're in a dark, dark place indeed."

The toll that campaigning takes on Claire is clear.

As journalists, we often talk to people who have lost family members in tragic circumstances.

It always amazes me how they have the strength to go on to campaign, raise money, change laws and save lives.

The drive it must take, the effort they put in and the toll it takes on them perhaps isn't talked about enough.

"I've come out of debates and wanted to throw myself under a bus," she says simply.

"But the reality is, I'm sat in Parliament but tonight I'll be walking into an empty home.

"No shoes at the door to trip over, no trumpet playing, no arguments, no noise, nobody to hold my hand.

"So, yeah we've changed the law, but my life won't change.

"For this to be their legacy will be incredible."

"All you want from your kids is to be proud of you and say 'well done Mum'."

articles.title: Sin tierra ni luz solar: una antigua mina de carbón de Asturias cultiva wasabi en el primer invernadero subterráneo de España
articles.standfirst: El pozo Carrio, en Laviana, ensaya cultivos de alto valor en una galería que extrajo carbón hasta 2018
articles.summary: El pozo Carrio, en Laviana, ensaya cultivos de alto valor en una galería que extrajo carbón hasta 2018
articles.body: Durante más de un siglo, las entrañas de las cuencas mineras asturianas fueron sinónimo de carbón y oscuridad. Cuando las minas cerraron, aquellas galerías parecían condenadas al olvido. Pero en una de ellas ha empezado a brotar una segunda vida inesperada. Se trata de la galería La Raya, en el pozo Carrio, en Laviana, una explotación propiedad de Hunosa que extrajo carbón hasta 2018. Su antigua bocamina alberga ahora el primer invernadero subterráneo de España, un proyecto piloto impulsado por el Servicio Regional de Investigación y Desarrollo Agroalimentario (SERIDA), la Consejería de Ciencia y la empresa Cantábrica Agricultura. Las plantas crecen mediante hidroponía, una técnica que prescinde del suelo, con iluminación LED y en un ambiente controlado. Los especialistas destacan que las minas ofrecen unas condiciones de humedad y temperatura muy estables, a salvo del tiempo exterior. La instalación cuenta con cuatro zonas de cultivo vertical donde se ensayan brotes, hierbas aromáticas, hojas verdes, rúcula, setas y hongos. Pero las grandes protagonistas son tres especies de alto valor: el wasabi, el guisante lágrima, muy apreciado y con una temporada de cosecha muy corta, y la salicornia, una planta capaz de crecer en ambientes salinos. “Algunos cultivos como la salicornia y el guisante lágrima se han desarrollado muy bien”, ha celebrado la directora del SERIDA, Mamen Oliván, que también destaca el éxito con el wasabi y los hongos. El objetivo ahora es identificar los cultivos más prometedores y aumentar su producción para generar actividad económica. No es una cuestión menor: tras el cierre de la minería del carbón, Asturias busca nuevos usos para miles de kilómetros de galerías subterráneas. El biólogo Javier Espina, técnico responsable del proyecto, plantea incluso que estas instalaciones puedan servir “a modo de refugio climático” o como banco de pruebas para futuros cultivos en la Luna.

articles.title: Ryanair lanza un dardo a sus pasajeros por el panettone de Dabiz Muñoz: “Pagáis por esto, pero no 8 euros por un asiento”
articles.standfirst: El dulce navideño mostrado en ‘El Hormiguero’ ha reabierto el debate sobre lo que estamos dispuestos a pagar
articles.summary: El dulce navideño mostrado en ‘El Hormiguero’ ha reabierto el debate sobre lo que estamos dispuestos a pagar
articles.body: Tras la inflación, quejarse por un suplemento de ocho euros al reservar un asiento en un avión. La comparación está servida y promete levantar ampollas entre los viajeros. El nuevo dulce navideño de Dabiz Muñoz, bautizado como Aliento de Dragón, se ha convertido en uno de los temas de conversación por su precio y su llamativa receta. Una situación que da pie a una reflexión muy del estilo de Ryanair: ¿por qué algunos gastos se aceptan sin rechistar mientras otros provocan indignación? El panettone del cocinero madrileño cuesta 46 euros por una pieza de 1,1 kilos y podrá adquirirse a través del Club del Gourmet de El Corte Inglés. Su lanzamiento está previsto para el 16 de noviembre y la producción será limitada. La elaboración destaca por su masa negra, coloreada con carbón vegetal, y una combinación de cacao, mantequilla tostada, chocolate blanco y cerezas amarenas. La polémica invita a comparar dos formas muy diferentes de entender el gasto. Por un lado, un producto gastronómico de autor que apuesta por ingredientes seleccionados, una elaboración artesanal y una imagen exclusiva. Por otro, los servicios adicionales de las aerolíneas económicas, que permiten personalizar el precio final del billete según las necesidades de cada pasajero. La frase “Pagáis por esto, pero no 8 euros por un asiento” funciona como una provocación dirigida a quienes están dispuestos a gastar en productos premium, pero consideran excesivo pagar un suplemento para elegir dónde sentarse durante un vuelo. No obstante, se trata de una comparación planteada como crítica y no de una declaración verificada de Ryanair sobre el panettone de Muñoz. El debate también pone sobre la mesa el valor que cada consumidor atribuye a su dinero. Mientras algunos justifican los 46 euros por la originalidad de la receta y el trabajo que requiere, otros consideran que el precio es demasiado elevado para un dulce navideño. En cualquier caso, la comparación evidencia una contradicción habitual en los hábitos de consumo: el precio puede percibirse de forma muy distinta dependiendo de lo que se compra y de las expectativas que genera. ¿Pagar casi 50 euros por un panettone es darse un capricho o un lujo innecesario? ¿Y ocho euros por elegir asiento, un abuso o un servicio opcional? La respuesta depende de cada bolsillo, pero la polémica está servida.
